newsitem.title: CHINA: China will take beating if backward - general.
newsitem.headline: China will take beating if backward - general.

text.p: One of Beijing's top military figures on Friday warned officers at a seminar celebrating Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule that China would take a beating at the hands of foreign forces if it were poor and backward.

"History in the past 100 years tells us once again that we will take a beating if we are poor and backward," the Xinhua news agency quoted General Zhang Zhen, a vice-chairman of the Communist Party's Central Military Commission, as saying.
"The nation will be humiliated and its sovereignty forfeited," Zhang told about 350 officers attending the seminar held just 11 days before Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule.
Britain defeated China in the 19th-century Opium Wars, forcing it to sign a series of unequal treaties under which Britain took Hong Kong and won the right to export opium to China.
"Only when we are rich, strong and prosperous can we defend national sovereignty and honour," Zhang said.

He brushed aside fears centring on the PLA soldiers who will be based in post-colonial Hong Kong, saying they were "devoted to their duties, law-abiding, civilised, practise strict discipline, are polite and will not encroach on the interests of the people to the slightest degree".
Images of the Chinese military crackdown on students demonstrating for democracy in Beijing in June 1989 remain vivid in the memories of many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million residents.
China denies it is a military threat to Asia or the rest of the world, but its army build-up in recent years has caused anxiety among its neighbours.
The sheer size of the three million-strong People's Liberation Army -- the world's biggest -- has caused uneasiness among China's neighbours.
China has been mired in a dispute with Asian neighbours over the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea and another dispute with Japan over a group of islands in the East China Sea.

It ruffled feathers in the region in March 1996 when it intimidated rival Taiwan by conducting missile tests and war games close to the island in the run-up to the first direct presidential elections there.
